nameStory: The Chestnut Slug gets its common name from its warm, reddish-brown coloration that resembles the rich hue of chestnuts fresh from their spiky shells. This earthy color helps it blend perfectly with fallen leaves and decomposing organic matter where it loves to hide. The name captures both its appearance and its preference for forested areas where chestnut trees might grow.
description: The Chestnut Slug is a small, soft-bodied land mollusk that glides along on its muscular foot, leaving a characteristic slime trail behind. These slugs are typically brownish to reddish-brown in color and reach about 1-2 inches in length when fully extended. Like all land slugs, they breathe air through a visible breathing pore and can retreat their tentacles when threatened. They're relatively recent arrivals to New England, having spread from their native southern Italy over the past century.

idTips.label: Chestnut-brown color
idTips.description: The body ranges from warm brown to reddish-brown, sometimes with a slightly mottled appearance that feels smooth and moist to the touch

idTips.label: Slime trail
idTips.description: Leaves a clear, sticky mucus trail that feels slippery between your fingers and can be seen glistening on surfaces

idTips.label: Breathing pore
idTips.description: Look for a round opening on the right side of the body near the front - this pneumostome opens and closes visibly as the slug breathes

idTips.label: Smooth skin texture
idTips.description: The skin feels remarkably smooth and wet, without the bumpy or ridged texture found on some other slug species

idTips.label: Retractable tentacles
idTips.description: Four tentacles that can be pulled completely inside the head when touched - the upper pair has tiny black eyes at the tips

habitat: Chestnut Slugs prefer moist, shaded areas with rich organic matter, often found under logs, leaf litter, or mulch in gardens and woodlands. They thrive in areas with consistent moisture like compost piles, around building foundations, and in well-watered flower beds. You'll rarely see them in dry, sunny locations as they need constant humidity to keep their skin from drying out.

seasonality.spring: Active as temperatures warm and soil moisture increases from snowmelt. Look for them emerging from winter hiding spots under logs or deep mulch.
seasonality.summer: Most active during humid nights and early mornings, retreating to cool, moist hiding places during hot days. Peak feeding and reproduction season.
seasonality.fall: Continue feeding actively before winter, often seen more frequently as they search for overwintering sites. Still active during mild, wet autumn weather.
seasonality.winter: Largely inactive, hiding deep in leaf litter, under logs, or below the frost line. May emerge briefly during winter thaws in protected areas.

funFact: This slug was a botanical detective mystery for decades - scientists thought they knew what species it was until 2011, when DNA evidence revealed that slugs worldwide weren't the Mediterranean species everyone assumed, but were actually a completely different species that needed a new name!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with the Milky Slug, which is similar in size but typically grayer and produces more noticeable white mucus when disturbed. Memory trick: 'Chestnut brown, Milky white' - think about the mucus color and overall body tone to tell them apart.
contextualKnowledge: This species illustrates how modern DNA analysis is revolutionizing our understanding of biodiversity - what scientists thought was a well-known Mediterranean slug turned out to be a case of mistaken identity lasting over a century. The real surprise was discovering that the 'familiar' species was actually undescribed by science until 2011.
compareHints: Compared to its relatives in New England, the Chestnut Slug is distinguished by its warm brown coloration - the Milky Slug tends to be grayer and produces more obvious white mucus, while the Meadow Slug is typically smaller and paler. The Chestnut Slug's consistently brownish color and smooth texture make it the most 'chestnut-like' of the three common Deroceras species in our region.

relatedSpecies.distinction: The milky slug is smaller than the meadow slug and produces much more noticeable white mucus when disturbed.
Compared to its close relatives, the Meadow Slug is distinguished by its completely smooth skin and preference for open habitats.
